items.before: Since the examination was only a week away, the teacher
items.after: all the chapters carefully and practise the model questions every day.
items.explanation: “Suggest” is not followed by an object plus “to”; it takes a that-clause with the bare verb: “suggested that we revise”.

items.after: the late delivery of the order and called the supplier to complain at once.
items.explanation: The adjective “angry” takes “about” before the thing that causes the anger, so “angry about the late delivery” is correct; “of”, “to”, “for” and “from” do not collocate with it.

items.after: , we will begin the installation on Friday morning and finish it over the weekend.
items.explanation: The sentence is already correct: a likely future condition takes the present simple in the if-clause and “will” in the main clause. The replacements mix tenses in the conditional.

items.before: He has been working in this company
items.after: and hopes to be promoted to a senior position soon.
items.explanation: “For” is used with a length of time (“for five years”), while “since” is used with a starting point.

items.after: to the weekly meeting and promised that it would not happen again.
items.explanation: “Apologise for” is followed by a gerund, so the correct form is “for being late”.

items.after: to the office yesterday because he had a high fever and needed complete rest.
items.explanation: After the auxiliary “did not” the main verb stays in its base form: “did not go”.

items.after: gifts they received from their grandparents on the festival day.
items.explanation: The sentence is already correct: “delighted with” is the standard collocation for the thing that pleases. The other prepositions do not collocate with “delighted” here.

items.before: The airline staff asked the passengers how
items.after: they were carrying and weighed each bag at the counter.
items.explanation: “Luggage” is uncountable, so it takes “much” and has no plural form: “how much luggage”.

items.after: next door to us is a doctor at the district hospital and treats many patients.
items.explanation: The relative pronoun for a person is “who”, and it takes a singular verb because “woman” is singular: “who lives”.

items.before: The harvest this year is not
items.after: last year's, mainly because the rains arrived very late.
items.explanation: An equal comparison is formed with “as ... as”, so “not as good as last year's” is correct.

items.sentence: All candidates must ______ their mobile phones before the written examination begins.
items.explanation: “Switch off” means to turn a device off, which is the sensible instruction before an examination. The other phrasal verbs make no sense with “mobile phones” here.

items.sentence: I would have attended the seminar if I ______ about it earlier.
items.explanation: A third conditional pairs “would have” in the main clause with the past perfect in the if-clause, so “had known” is needed.

items.sentence: I have been trying to ______ the topic of a salary revision with my manager for weeks, but he is always busy.
items.explanation: “Bring up” means to raise a subject for discussion, which suits “the topic of a salary revision”. The others mean cause, reduce, trigger or persuade.

items.sentence: Everyone says that Meena ______ her mother, as she has the same warm smile and gentle voice.
items.explanation: “Take after” means to resemble a parent or relative, which is explained by the shared smile and voice. The other phrasal verbs do not express resemblance.

items.after: sharply this month because the rains damaged the crops.
items.explanation: The subject is the singular noun “price”, not “vegetables”, so the verb must be singular: “has gone up”.

items.after: of all the boys in his class and plays in the school basketball team.
items.explanation: A comparison among more than two people needs the superlative, so “the tallest of all the boys” is correct; “the taller” compares only two.
